entries.previousTitle: Continued Influence Effect – when misinformation sticks, even after being debunked
entries.title: Continued Influence Effect – when corrected information still shapes reasoning
entries.description:
The Continued Influence Effect happens when false or outdated information still affects later reasoning after a person has been told that it is wrong. A correction can help and the old information can still leave a trace at the same time.

Where can it show up?
- Breaking news: an early explanation is corrected, but people still use it when explaining what happened.
- Work and incident reviews: an initial root cause is ruled out, yet later discussion keeps returning to it.
- Everyday claims: you remember that a statement was corrected but still use part of the original story when judging a related question.

A better check
- State the correction clearly instead of only saying that the old claim is wrong.
- If the old claim filled an explanatory gap, give the best supported alternative explanation when one is available.
- Keep important corrections easy to find and repeat them when needed.
- Do not call incomplete updating a backfire effect. Backfire requires the false belief itself to become stronger after the correction.
entries.reason: The legacy page treated persistence after correction as if the false claim simply remained believed. The reviewed literature supports a narrower distinction: corrections often improve accuracy while misinformation can still influence later inference, and that is not the same as backfire.
